Presidential Gubernatorial A tale of two emergencies: Why Nigeria does not need new science, By Adewale Adeyemo No one should die at a hospital gate. No one should die on the hard shoulder of a Nigerian expressway, while bystanders do what paramedics should. by Premium Times October 31, 2026 Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Add us on Google
Nigeria trains excellent doctors and exports many of them. What it lacks is the chain that carries a collapsing person to one of them in time… That chain can be built. Stabilise first and bill later, through a funded federal scheme that reimburses hospitals that comply. Enforce Section 20, so that refusal carries real consequences. Build urgent care centres along the major expressways and in the cities where the crashes and collapses actually happen. Give NEHA the mandate to run them. Set up coordination that knows, in real time, which emergency unit has a bed, a scanner and a team. Staff and stock those units round the clock.
On 15 September 2025, in Park City, Utah, a police dog called Bruno went over the edge of a highway overpass. He broke two legs and fractured his jaw. An officer knelt on the road and held him still. A helicopter flew him to a specialist hospital in Salt Lake City. Surgeons operated the next day. Soon after, he limped out past staff who lined the corridor and clapped as he passed.
On 14 October 2025, in Ibadan, the gospel singer, Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, known to his many fans as Toluwanisings , slumped in the early hours. His media aide, Babadunni Gbolabo said that eight hospitals turned him away. His family confirmed his death that same morning.
Eight doors. Eight refusals. Somewhere between them, the time he had left ran out.
TOLUWANISINGS WAS NOT THE FIRST THIS YEAR. HE WILL NOT BE THE LAST.
On 29 December 2025, Anthony Joshua, the two-time world heavyweight champion, was in a crash on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway at Makun, Ogun State. His close friends, Sina Ghami and Kevin “Latif” Ayodele, died at the scene. Joshua survived with minor injuries. The world watched images of a global sportsman being pulled from the wreckage by bystanders. Not paramedics. Not a trained first-response crew. Bystanders.
Follow us on Google News and never miss breaking stories, investigations, and in-depth reporting.
There was no air ambulance. No roadside stabilisation unit. No equipped centre within reach of that stretch of road at that hour. President Bola Tinubu called Joshua personally. The world’s attention came and went. The infrastructure gap stays.
Nigeria recorded 5,421 road traffic deaths in 2024 alone. The Joshua crash was not an outlier. It was a famous version of what happens quietly, somewhere on a Nigerian road, every single day.
Over 11,000 kilometres separate Salt Lake City from Ibadan. The real distance is measured in minutes, in money, and in who answers when you knock.
This is not a quarrel with Bruno. He deserved every hand that reached for him. What moves me is what was already in place before he fell. A trained responder. An evacuation plan. A hospital ready to receive him. An institution ready to pay the bill.
Sina Ghami and Latif Ayodele had a famous friend, a working mobile phone, and the attention of a Nigerian president. None of that bought them a stabilising clinician on the hard shoulder of the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.
We like to believe that illness alone decides who lives. Often, the system does. In emergency medicine, the clock is part of the disease. In a major stroke, the brain loses an estimated 1.9 million neurons for every minute without treatment. In major trauma, the first hour decides outcomes. The same injury can be survivable in one city and fatal in another. Human physiology does not change at the border. The road to care does.
AND YET THE SKILL IS AT HOME. I HAVE WATCHED IT SAVE SOMEONE CLOSE TO ME.
On 16 July 2025, I sat thousands of miles away, gripping my phone. A relative had arrived at University College Hospital, Ibadan, at 11 a.m. Moribund. A blocked artery was starving the brain.
My heart sank. Every clinician knows what that number means. The standard window for clot-dissolving treatment closes at four-and-a-half hours. After that, the risk of bleeding into the brain rises sharply and the tissue that can still be saved shrinks.
The neurologist did not take the easy refusal. He read the scan carefully. He weighed what could still be saved against what could be lost. He spoke with us. Then he went ahead.
The country already has pieces of the puzzle… What is missing sits in the middle. A dedicated tier of Urgent and Emergency Care Centres, physically positioned on the expressways and in the major cities where people actually collapse. Walk-in. Specialist-led. Twenty-four hours. Rapid diagnostics on site. Air stabilisation capability. The facility that the NEMSAS ambulance drives the patient to. The place the bystanders on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway could have reached in time.
It was 1:53 p.m. Two hours and fifty-three minutes after arrival. About seven-and-a-half hours after the first symptoms.
Today, my relative walks, runs, talks and drives, with no deficit you would notice.
That was textbook hyperacute stroke care. Delivered in Ibadan. By Nigerian hands.
Our access came through people. Medical school classmates and a senior mentor who are like family picked up the phone, made the calls and stayed with us until it was done. I will carry that debt for the rest of my life.
But I must be honest about what that means. It means privilege. Our network carried us past the cash deposits, the delays and the gridlock that kill ordinary Nigerians at the gate. And behind the right team on duty, a working scanner and the drug in stock, I believe, sat the grace of God.
Grace should not have to stand in for a system. No Nigerian should need the right phone numbers to survive.
Section 20 of the National Health Act 2014 states that a health care provider, health worker or health establishment shall not refuse a person emergency medical treatment for any reason. The penalty is a fine of ₦100,000, up to six months in prison, or both.
On paper, the right exists. At a locked gate before dawn, it does not.
The reasons are known. Hospitals that treat first are often never paid. Emergency units run short of staff, beds and blood. No one tracks which hospital has space. Families are left to drive from gate to gate, guessing, while the clock runs. On expressways, there is no one to call at all.
The country already has pieces of the puzzle. The National Emergency Medical Service and Ambulance System (NEMSAS), launched in 2022 and now operational across 33 states and the FCT, dispatches ambulances and funds the first 48 hours of care through the Basic Health Care Provision Fund. The Federal Road Safety Corps patrols the expressways. The National Emergency Management Agency responds to disasters. The National Primary Health Care Development Agency runs primary care at the ward level.
What is missing sits in the middle. A dedicated tier of Urgent and Emergency Care Centres, physically positioned on the expressways and in the major cities where people actually collapse. Walk-in. Specialist-led. Twenty-four hours. Rapid diagnostics on site. Air stabilisation capability. The facility that the NEMSAS ambulance drives the patient to. The place the bystanders on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway could have reached in time.
Every advanced nation has this tier. The United Kingdom has 999 and Walk-in Urgent Treatment Centres. The United States and Canada has 911 as their national emergency number and Level 1 trauma centres. Rwanda has SAMU, co-funded by the WHO and the World Bank, with ambulances and air units covering the whole country. Nigeria has the ambulance but not the destination.
This gap needs an owner. The clean answer is a National Emergency Healthcare Authority (NEHA), a dedicated federal agency that establishes, regulates and operates urgent care infrastructure nationally. It would absorb NEMSAS as its dispatch arm, coordinate with the FRSC on expressway positioning, work alongside NEMA on mass casualties, and sit under the Federal Ministry of Health with independent funding. One agency. One mandate. One accountable name when a Nigerian dies at a gate.
The alternative is what we have now. Six overlapping bodies, no single owner, and a Toluwanisings every month that we do not read about because he was not a gospel singer.
A rotation model that offers diaspora consultants eight to twelve weeks a year in a well-run urgent care centre, with proper accommodation, family-friendly scheduling, and professional indemnity, would attract hundreds. Not because they are paid more. But because they are finally offered a way to serve home that fits their stage of life. The older cohort will anchor the specialist teaching. The younger ones, still mid-career abroad, would add shorter rotations when they come to see loved ones.
A federal agency is only as good as the clinicians who stand inside its buildings at 3 a.m. This is where Nigeria has a quiet advantage it has never used properly.
Nigerian-trained physicians fill senior consultant posts across the NHS, the Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, Toronto General, Mount Sinai. Thousands of them. Many are now in their late 50s and 60s. In the Western systems where they practise, the pattern at that age is well known. Full clinical rotas are swapped for teaching, mentorship, governance, and part-time consulting. Children are grown. Mortgages are paid. Personal needs are smaller. What rises is the desire to give back something that lasts.
Most of them already return home for two or three weeks each year. Family visits, funerals, weddings. Almost none of that time is converted into structured clinical work at home. If the state built the right platform, that calculus can change.
A rotation model that offers diaspora consultants eight to twelve weeks a year in a well-run urgent care centre, with proper accommodation, family-friendly scheduling, and professional indemnity, would attract hundreds. Not because they are paid more. But because they are finally offered a way to serve home that fits their stage of life. The older cohort will anchor the specialist teaching. The younger ones, still mid-career abroad, would add shorter rotations when they come to see loved ones. A working holiday with purpose rather than guilt.
This is how the brain drain begins to reverse. Not by begging physicians to come back permanently, which few will, but by letting them come back regularly, meaningfully, in formats that respect the lives they have built. Over a generation, the clinical teaching, the governance culture, and the standard of care seeded by returning diaspora consultants build the lasting institutions Nigeria needs.
Until those institutions stand on their own, the diaspora is the bridge.
None of this works without those who stayed. The Nigerian consultants, registrars, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, laboratory scientists, radiographers and allied health professionals who have carried the system through every power cut, every strike, every unpaid month, are the backbone of any future. The diaspora is the bridge. The home workforce is the ground the bridge stands on.
A model that threatens their livelihoods will fail, and deserves to. A model that strengthens them will succeed. The pay structures, the training opportunities, the promotion pathways, and the clinical leadership roles must be designed to lift Nigerian clinicians first. Diaspora rotations should supplement, teach, mentor and share, never displace. Every returning consultant should see herself as a visitor in the house of colleagues who kept the lights on, not as the owner of a new wing. The welcome goes both ways. Those at home must open the door. Those abroad must know they are coming into someone’s workplace, not building their own. Get this balance right and both sides win. Get it wrong and the diaspora becomes just one more imposition on a workforce that has already carried too much.
It looks like an ambulance that comes when you call. A hospital that stabilises first and asks for money later. A law that is enforced. A trained paramedic on a stretch of expressway where strangers currently kneel over the dying.
Talent is spread evenly across the world. Safety nets are not.
Nigeria trains excellent doctors and exports many of them. What it lacks is the chain that carries a collapsing person to one of them in time.
That chain can be built. Stabilise first and bill later, through a funded federal scheme that reimburses hospitals that comply. Enforce Section 20, so that refusal carries real consequences. Build urgent care centres along the major expressways and in the cities where the crashes and collapses actually happen. Give NEHA the mandate to run them. Set up coordination that knows, in real time, which emergency unit has a bed, a scanner and a team. Staff and stock those units round the clock.
None of this needs new science. It needs will, money and follow-through.
Until then, survival in Nigeria will remain a lottery of luck, location and who you know.
No one should die at a hospital gate. No one should die on the hard shoulder of a Nigerian expressway, while bystanders do what paramedics should.
Adewale Adeyemo, a London-trained consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist with a special interest in clinical risk management and patient safety, writes from Canada.
